value.overview: The Slaty-backed Nightingale-Thrush (Catharus fuscater) is a secretive songbird of humid mountain forests in Central and South America. It usually stays in dense understory and on the forest floor, where its dark plumage blends with shadowed vegetation. Its clear, low, flute-like song is often easier to hear than the bird is to see. Costa Rica supports an important northern population, especially in the Caribbean-facing highlands and selected Pacific-slope mountain forests.
value.classification: The Slaty-backed Nightingale-Thrush belongs to the thrush family, Turdidae, and the genus Catharus. It is a passerine bird. Several geographically distinct populations and subspecies are recognized, and the taxonomy of the wider Catharus fuscater complex has been under scientific review.
value.identification: A medium-sized, mostly dark thrush with slate-gray to dusky upperparts, a darker head, and somewhat paler gray underparts. Adults have a conspicuous orange to yellow-orange eye-ring, a dark bill, and orange or yellowish legs. The throat may appear whitish gray and subtly marked, while immature birds are browner and more heavily mottled. Its song consists of leisurely, simple, flute-like phrases, often delivered from concealed vegetation in the dim understory.
value.rangeHabitat: The species has a disjunct range from Costa Rica and Panama through the Andes of Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador, Peru, and Bolivia. It inhabits humid montane evergreen forest, cloud forest, dense streamside vegetation, and thick understory, generally from about 800 to 2,300 meters in Costa Rica. In Costa Rica it is a resident and is locally common on the Caribbean slope from the Panamanian border north toward the Cordillera de Guanacaste. It also occurs locally on the Pacific slope, especially in the Cordillera de Talamanca and around Dota, often at somewhat higher elevations.
value.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and generally considered a year-round resident throughout its range. It may make short local movements in response to food, weather, or breeding conditions, but it is not a regular long-distance migrant.
value.breeding: Breeding information is limited, but in Costa Rica the breeding season is reported mainly from April through August. The nest is a sturdy cup made from rootlets, plant fibers, leaves, and moss, usually placed in a fork or dense vegetation in the lower understory, approximately 0.5 to 3 meters above the ground. Clutches generally contain two pale blue or blue-green eggs with darker markings. The female apparently performs most nest construction, while details of incubation and chick development remain incompletely documented.
value.dietFeeding: The Slaty-backed Nightingale-Thrush is an omnivorous forest-floor forager. It eats beetles, ants, spiders, other small invertebrates, and a variety of berries and other small fruits. It searches through leaf litter and low vegetation, frequently in shaded places near streams or dense undergrowth. In Costa Rica it has also been observed following army-ant swarms, taking prey items disturbed by the moving ants.
value.behavior: This thrush is usually solitary or found in pairs and spends much of its time walking or hopping quietly through dark understory and leaf litter. It can be difficult to detect because it remains close to the ground and often stays hidden, although it may sing repeatedly from a concealed perch. Its song is soft but distinctive, with separated, melodious phrases. It is active during the day and may defend a breeding territory through song.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population size has not been reliably quantified and is believed to be decreasing, although the species remains fairly common or locally common in parts of its range, including Costa Rica.
